subject: Private GPU pool: throughput profiles, failover & escalation matrix
messages:
From: Tom Harris <tom.harris@rackcentral.com>
To: olga_petrov@redwood.com
Cc: infra@rackcentral.com
Date: Mon, 30 Jun 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Midtown Analytics — on-prem pool sizing inputs and target SLAs

Hi Olga,

Thanks again for taking this on. Midtown has asked us to validate throughput and a short escalation matrix for their private deployment (on-prem VPC) before procurement signs off. They published expected production traffic in the attached CSV (privgpu_throughput_profiles_v1.csv). High-level ask:

- Sustained inference target: 3,500 qps (short requests, avg 120 tokens per request).
- Burst tolerance: up to 9,000 qps for 5–10 minute windows once per day.
- P95 latency target: <= 220ms for the 120-token profile (end-to-end at the customer edge).
- Cold-start tolerance: can accept 10–15s cold start for node spin-up but want warm-pool ramping < 60s.

We also attached their network outline (network_topology_rackcentral_v2.pdf). Main concerns RackCentral raised: top-of-rack NICs and oversubscription, storage for KV cache warmups, and whether queueing should live at the infra layer or in the Redwood agent.

Can you confirm what realistic GPU mix we should propose (A100/H100 vs L4) and a simple escalation matrix (who gets paged at different degradation levels) so procurement can advance?

Tom
Senior Solutions Architect
RackCentral Solutions

Attachment: privgpu_throughput_profiles_v1.csv (CSV, 18 KB)
Attachment: network_topology_rackcentral_v2.pdf (PDF, 220 KB)

From: olga_petrov@redwood.com
To: Tom Harris <tom.harris@rackcentral.com>
Cc: jonas_weber@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 30 Jun 2025 10:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Midtown Analytics — on-prem pool sizing inputs and target SLAs

Tom — thanks for the data. I took a first pass through the CSV and sketched a conservative sizing profile + operational playbook. High-level notes below; I attached a short run-card (escalation_matrix_draft.xlsx).

Summary recommendations (first pass):
- GPU mix: H100s (for baseline) if Midtown wants consistent p95 < 220ms at 120 tokens. H100 gives better latency headroom for quantized LLMs with large KV caches; fallback pool of A100 80GB is acceptable if H100 inventory is constrained. L4s are only cost-effective for small, single-turn embedding-like workloads — not for this token/latency profile.
- Baseline capacity: design for sustained 3,500 qps with 30% headroom => plan GPU allocation equal to ~4.5k qps capability. Rough mapping: with our inference profiles, one H100 can sustain ~900 qps for 120-token avg (with batching/kv cache). So ~5 H100s baseline, plan 2 extra as warm capacity for absorb/burst.
- Burst strategy: staged warm-pool + staged autoscale. For 9k qps bursts, target warm-pool to cover first 60% of burst (~5.4k qps) with remaining added via fast spin-up (expected 30–90s) across spare nodes. That implies keeping 6–7 nodes in warm state when burst probability > 10%.
- Network: require 100Gbps uplinks on rack aggregation layer (or 25Gb * 4 with non-oversubscription) to avoid NIC saturation during bursts. KV cache preload to local SSDs (NVMe) to avoid NFS thrash.
- Queue placement: we recommend infra-layer rate-limiter + Redwood agent admission control; infra queue should be conservative (short queueing window 100–200ms) while agent-level queue handles token-level batching to preserve latency SLOs.

Open questions for RackCentral/Midtown:
1) Do they prefer H100-only or mixed A100 fallback?
2) What's their preferred cold-start max time (they said 10–15s). We need to model spin-up times for their hypervisor (they listed VMware ESXi v8).
3) Do they have preference on warm-pool resident nodes vs. burst in separate racks? (cross-rack warming adds network egress concerns).

Next actions I propose:
- Jonas: can you validate the 900 qps/H100 mapping with synthesis numbers and add a network bottleneck test plan?
- Karthik: can you draft a simple cost/time delta for H100 vs A100 baseline and an ops runbook for warm-pool thresholds?

I'll hold until you both comment; then I'll send a 1-page to RackCentral and schedule a 30-min call.

—
Olga Petrov
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
olga_petrov@redwood.com

Attachment: escalation_matrix_draft.xlsx (XLSX, 12 KB)

From: jonas_weber@redwood.com

Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, Tom Harris <tom.harris@rackcentral.com>
Date: Tue, 01 Jul 2025 11:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Midtown Analytics — on-prem pool sizing inputs and target SLAs

Olga / Tom — I validated the latency/throughput mapping in a local profiled run using a quantized LLM that roughly mirrors Midtown's token distribution (120-token avg):

- Measured sustained per-H100 throughput (with continuous batching and KV cache warm): 880–930 qps, p50 latency ~55ms, p95 ~180–210ms depending on batching window. Numbers assume NVMe-backed local cache and no NIC oversubscription.
- A100 80GB baseline measured 650–700 qps in the same profile (p95 increases ~30–40ms).

Sizing math I used (rounded):
- Target sustained 3,500 qps with 30% headroom -> design for 4,550 qps.
- Using 900 qps/H100 -> 5.1 nodes -> round up to 6 H100 nodes for baseline (6*900 = 5,400 qps capacity).
- Warm spare nodes: keep 2 nodes hot (to absorb immediate spikes).
- Burst target 9,000 qps: with 6 baseline + 2 warm = 8 nodes * 900 = 7,200 qps. To reach 9k we need ~10 nodes total. So plan for cold capacity to spin 2 additional nodes within 60–90s.

Operational notes:
- Warm-pool policy: keep warm-pool size variable by time-of-day and recent burst probability. Example: during peak windows (per CSV) keep warm-pool at 3 nodes; off-peak, scale warm-pool to 1.
- Admission control: enforce hard concurrency limits per-tenant and fast-fail at agent level when in overload mode to prevent node thrash. Return 429 with explanatory retry-after.
- Network test plan: simulate 9k qps traffic from synthetic clients across the top-of-rack with packet-capture to validate no bufferbloat. Test LOCALLY with 100Gbps NIC to verify no tail-latency degradation under KV cache misses.

I will attach the raw test logs and a short script for the synthetic driver in the Drive link.

—
Jonas Weber
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference
